header.title: Carmen Apologeticum: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Commodianus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's stoa0096.stoa004.opp-lat2, from Open Greek and Latin's CSEL (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0096.stoa004.opp-la: Line 2: lacuna marked in the edition (* *); sense of 'tulerit' uncertain. Line 8: 'fni' read as 'fere' or similar ('almost'); 'Marsus' = a Marsian, i.e. a snake-charmer/sorcerer. Line 21 is marked corrupt (†) in the edition and is unmetrical; translation is tentative. Line 55: sense obscure; 'erratur' construed loosely. Line 62: 'austris' (south winds) is odd; some read 'aliis' or similar. Line 73: 'ad escam' uncertain. Line 77: 'missam' taken as military discharge (missio). Line 116: construction elliptical (infinitive without governing verb). Line 154: 'priorque' taken as 'first'. Line 155: subject and sense of 'per ipsos' unclear. Scanning errors corrected: 'storias' = historias (151), 'sicat' = sicut, 'prios' = prius, 'torrem' = turrem, 'nna' = una, 'nario' = vario; stray marks (I, ., :, \') omitted.

174 'per latices animae' (through the waters of the soul) is obscure. 184 'tempore partito ... ablato' is difficult; rendered tentatively. 196 'in hominem depretiatur' taken as 'would be held cheap in [his] manhood'. 204 and 233: stray '7' omitted as a printing mark. 227 the edition's unclosed parenthesis is ignored; 'de tuba' taken as 'as with a trumpet'. 263 'stadia' (course, place) uncertain. 281-283: lacuna; 281 restorations translated, 282 lost, 283 fragmentary and its sense unclear. 307 'perseueraris' read for the misprint. 345 'Malachiel' is Malachi; the name means 'my angel/messenger', hence 'himself also an angel'.

347: 'acceptam' read as 'acceptum'. 371: the text quoted is Baruch 3:36–38, attributed by Commodian to Jeremiah; 'aequalis' may mean 'none is equal [to him]'. 375: sense obscure ('in occasum' = 'to the west'?). 377: Psalm 44 in the Latin numbering. 388: line obscure, perhaps corrupt; 'canentibus rostra elusissent' rendered literally. 390: 'seruus' presumably for 'seruitus'. 394: 'erint' for 'erunt'. 425: lacuna in the edition. 432: emended to 'scite' by the edition. 441: 'inrigat' rendered loosely as 'pours on'; sense uncertain (perhaps 'inrogat', 'imposes'). 449–450: quotation unidentified and the sense obscure. 455: 'more Saturni' unclear. 483–496: Wisdom 2:12–20, ascribed to Solomon. 506: 'cam' read as 'eam', with '(im)pletum' as the edition restores it.

519–520: the quotation attributed to Moses resembles Numbers 23:19 (Balaam's oracle). 531: 'nonum' read as 'nouum' (new). 548: 'diota' read as 'dicta'. 542: a lacuna in the text. 584: 'cor' is rendered 'mind'; the sense of the line is uncertain. 590: 'in Christo negauit' is taken as 'denied Christ'. 602: 'aegrotat' ('he is sick', presumably sick in soul) is obscure. 611: 'sacculo' (money-bag) may be a misreading of 'saeculo' (for the world). 626–628: the talking dog and lion come from the apocryphal Acts of Peter and Acts of Paul. 630: the infant's speech seems also to come from the Acts of Peter. 637: 'centriam' is corrupt; it is read as 'ceruicem' (neck). 638: the quoted objection has no close in the text. 652: this reference is missing from the stretch. 680: the construction is uncertain.

695 'tricesima': literally 'the thirtieth [days]'; the reference (Jewish new-moon or other monthly rites) is uncertain. 698: the construction is obscure; rendered literally. 724: sense uncertain; taken as the son squandering the estate to spite the father. 762 'strenia(m)': the edition's restoration; the word (cf. strena, festive gift; or strenuitas) is doubtful, rendered 'revelry'. 778 'Stulto<S> infatuant': text uncertain. 793 'solis in agone': obscure, literally 'in the contest/course of the sun'. 810: the leading '10' is a stray line number, omitted. 814 'ei parte': probably corrupt. 825 'praeceptus' read as 'praereptus' (snatched away). 831 'inuisum' may mean 'unseen' or 'hated'.

Many lines here rest on editorial restoration of a damaged text (985-986, 1027-1030, 1033-1034, 1039-1040); these are translated as restored. Line 1032 is largely lost and only its end can be translated. Line 877 'historia' is unclear (perhaps 'in this event/occasion'). Line 1001 lacks an expressed subject; 'trumpet' (tuba) is supplied from the feminine adjectives. In 1026 'Bapietur' is read as 'rapietur'. Line 988 is uncertain: 'sancti(s)' read as dative 'of the saints'. In 958 the sense of 'cetera surda' ('the rest were deaf/unheeding') is obscure. Line 951 'animam' taken as 'living creature'. Line 937 read 'ipsi' as 'with him'.

1048: 'illos' (1047) taken as Christ's crucifiers, raised to see his glory and then returned 'in imis' (to the depths). 1050–1051: text badly damaged; 1050 only partly legible, 1051 yields no connected sense (fragments '-nius sistic-'). 1057 echoes Psalm 54(55):16, 'descendant in infernum viventes'. 1058: the sentence continues beyond this stretch; 'living' supplied from context.

nodes.text: THE APOLOGETIC POEM OF COMMODIAN.
Who will be able properly to know the one God of the heavens,
Unless the one whom he has carried off * * from abominable error?
I was wandering, roaming in ignorance, caught by empty hope,
While the frenzy of my first youth was carrying me into the breezes.
I was lighter than chaff; as if a hundred heads were
On my shoulders, so I was borne headlong wherever [it took me].
Not enough: in these things, guilty as I was, I finally
Almost became a Marsian, chanting spells over malignant herbs.
But thanks to the Lord — my voice is not sufficient to render
So much — who at last shone light on the wretch as he wavered!
And I set about [reading] in the handed-down book of the law,
To find out what was there; at once a lamp shone for me.
Then indeed I recognised God, (the one) highest in the heights,
And therefore I urge such people to withdraw from error.
Who is a better physician than one who has suffered the burning of a wound?
Many indeed, brutish and unknowing, asleep in heart,
Set themselves to learn nothing; in the manner of wild beasts
They seek what they may plunder or on whose blood they may live.
So long as they delight to live as fattened pigs,
They heap up dishes like a burial mound, while they applaud their riches.
† They will be changed by poor clothing, by their disdains.
Surely what they eat more readily would suffice them.
If someone is fat with wealth, let it be his own; if he is worthy of Caesar,
Why does he, frail as he is, set his own things first and have regard for no one?
Rather let such a one share his goodness with all,
To whom the Highest has granted riches and lofty honours.
For I do not blame riches given by the Highest,
But he will be blameworthy who is puffed up over them.
I now therefore urge all, high and humble alike,
To read assiduously either these things or the other things of the law.
Look, since a short life has been entrusted to us;
Learn, you who are wise, why we who are born must die!
Why do we die dull-witted, what use was it to have seen the light?
If you inquire into nothing, this is to be present as the beasts are.
Surely the highest God set man over the fields,
Not a wild beast or a beast of the flock. Why should we make ourselves like them?
The Almighty wished man to offer him praises;
For this reason he himself taught us divine things to come.
And so that we should believe them, he did not merely sound them in word,
But also displayed mighty deeds when Pharaoh was deceived.
Not only did he do this: in the times of Noah also
He showed what he could do, since no one was seeking God.
Thereafter he began little by little to be present more gently,
Once the Flood had taken place, so that the earth could be filled again.
Already almost half of the six thousand years was passing,
And no one knew the Lord, and they were living at random.
But God, when he saw that the hearts of men were too much closed,
Speaks to Abraham, of whom Moses himself gives account.
He gave the law to the people when Pharaoh had been killed,
And the Lord himself foretold through him who he was.
Not content with a single prophetic voice does he declare himself,
But he called in many witnesses, who cry out about him.
This one, therefore, when you read the proclamations of many prophets,
You will find to have found flesh for our sake.
Hence there is error now, [as to whether] the Highest ordained such things,
And they as it were sneer, and do not know that they are laughed at by him!
Meanwhile I set down how I have read through the prophets,
And I teach the untaught where the hope of life should be placed.
What God did at the beginning and how he made each thing,
Moses has already taught; but we teach about Christ.
I am not a prophet, nor was I commanded to be a teacher,
But I lay open the predictions of the prophets to those straying before the south winds.
So you who are like me, whom the breeze carries off in haste,
Seek now the harbour, where there are no dangers.
The skilled farmer discerns the weather from afar
And, before it comes, withdraws under cover.
Be wise, see beforehand what is threatening,
And, before disasters come, provide for your safety.
Sloth is the business of boys, certainly not of the strong:
If this suits the untaught, it does not befit those mature in age.
Whatever part of mankind is not restrained, when old
Will be like a ham hardly salted: it will rot.
No one subdues a rock, except fire alone [acting] as fuel:
So stony men grow soft late, in Gehenna.
We cry out, in vain, to deaf storms that throw [it] back,
And we offer light, holding it out to the blind to no purpose.
A soldier stands at his discharge: one listens, and another shakes it off
And does not take the warnings to heart, but strays, lost.
Which one, now, does wrong (be judges of these!),
He who warns, or he who will not obey what is said?
I hope he is not guilty who obeys the word of Caesar,
But the proud man who opposes it loses his life.
Meanwhile, what is mine to do, I who strayed before, I show:
The right road to you who still stray in emptiness.
Yet you choose, pleasing your own judgement,
Which one would want, poison or the sweet cups of life!
Good and evil were created in this nature,
So that after death man may be proved, who is worthy of God.
Set about it now, whoever you are, to know eternal things:
Learn who God is, and in whose name he is present!
There is God almighty, one, created from himself,
Whom you will find below to be both great and humble himself.
He was set in the Word, known to himself alone,
Who is called Father and Son and Holy Spirit.
But from when he decided to compose the world with signs,
He set between a fire to be feared by the angels themselves.
Whom, however, he distributed, made of lesser power,
To rule the heavens and the earth and what is subject to the earth.
Him, therefore, not even the messengers themselves can discern,
What he is like or how great, except that they follow his commands.
His honour is hidden from us and from the angels themselves,
In that the majesty of God, what it is, is known to itself alone.
It shines back immense above the heavens and without end;
The whole is golden, which is like a fiery power.
There is God's vessel, only without known form;
Those are the secrets of the heavens known to God alone.
This is the unique glory of God, above all the angels;
This is God of eternal light, this the spirit of the age.
What he is like in his original state is seen by no one;
He is transfigured, as he wishes to show himself.
He offers himself visible to angels according to their form
And for man he becomes man; otherwise God is proved by the Word.
For this reason the form of so great a God cannot be discerned;
Whatever it is, it is one, alone in immeasurable light;
Where a face, eyes or mouth or limbs are noted,
Thence [he is said] to enclose the circle of the world in his fist.
But yet, when he wished it to be known of himself who he was,
From so great a divinity he made himself seen as comprehensible.
There are those to whom he appeared in fire, speaking with a voice;
He was taken up into flesh, whom no region could contain.
This God almighty, Lord of his own creation,
Though he is invisible, makes himself seen by some.
He who now takes form, (now) spreads himself into the breezes,
Whose beginning and end it is not lawful to seek.
This one is always God without beginning and without end,
Who, before he made the heaven, was borne on through the age;
Whatever the heaven holds, he looks out on everywhere from heaven
And penetrates the whole with his eyes and hears with his ears.
It pleased him, therefore, [to make] the fleshly course of the world,
So that the everlasting majesty alone might be exalted.
For what was before, it is now a hard thing to relate;
Though it be written down, let us not be concerned with those things.
Since we cannot touch all of these things that we see,
Who will be able to know what is beyond the end of the Ocean?
We see the heaven too, but what is done inside there
It is given to no one to know, until the end of the age comes.
Let it suffice only to know the promises about the future;
Let us strive eagerly toward them, devoted with all our mind.
Just as the bird Phoenix contrives to be reborn from death,
It gives us an example, that we can rise after death;
This God almighty urges us most of all to believe,
That a time will come for the dead to live again;
Though one be now dust, though the bones lie bared,
The man who was dead will one day be made whole,
And the grace then will be greater (than) that of this age;
There will then be no pain nor tears in our body,
The flesh will not receive the sword, no blister will rise.
This God will establish, so that his glory may be greater.
He had made the first man to be eternal,
But he fell headlong into death, having neglected the commands.
On account of which God arranged that there should be such great histories,
So that he might wipe away all the devices of the devil.
God had given this angel as ruler on earth:
Who, while he envied man, himself perished, and first.
Meanwhile he discerns the just through their own deeds,
And reserves the criminal Cain in Gehenna.
The whole human race began to dwell in wickedness,
Not regarding who their creator was.
Because God on high bore this with indignation,
He resolves to destroy almost all created things.
It is said and read that Noah was freed from the water;
The rest perished in the heavenly Flood.
From then, as at the beginning, the earth is gradually filled again.
The former crime ceased, but another disaster clung.
Fools set about building a tower beneath the stars,
So that by it, as it were, they could ascend the heavens.
When God saw this being done under one speech,
He came down and caused them to speak different tongues.
These he then scattered, separated, through the islands of the earth,
So that they became nations speaking various languages.
Then the untaught race led a life of savagery;
no one knew God, no one reasoned about life.
For that reckless one had crept into the unformed [people]
through the waters of the soul; he corrupted their harsh minds
and persuaded them by guile to love unspeakable unions,
to live by plunder, in joy at blood that was shed.
This glory fools pursue for a short time;
from which no pardon frees them, by saying they were led astray.
If the adulterer persuades, the fault is yours for following such a one;
he does not condemn you, but you condemn yourself of your own will.
The untaught wandered by the deceit of the ancient enemy,
forgetting the Lord, following wicked works.
So that such ravaging by the robber should not go on long,
at an appointed time [God] at last took pity, [the time] being ended.
It pleased him to speak with one out of many,
so as to make a people beloved by its crossing over to him.
From that [man] the profane began to know one God
and to become a people according to God's decrees.
For Rebecca had separated two peoples from herself:
this one was made first, the other so as to succeed it.
In Egypt Israel first grew up as a nursling;
from there God led them out with Moses as leader,
through whom he gave them the law on Mount Sinai,
so that our posterity might know the one Lord.
Then he ordered prophets from among them to declare
that God in [his] manhood would be held cheap by them.
The Lord had led them into the promised land,
so that there they might live under the law, until he himself should come.
A race ungrateful for good things would not bear the yoke of the precepts,
but rather, rolled back into ancient wickedness, it flourished;
nor has it ever ceased: today too it is held to be such;
passing God by, it prefers the luxuries of the world.
This the Lord most of all compels his beloved to shun;
he warns them beforehand to be wholly cut off from the world.
If he called [us] sons, let us dwell in his holy things;
why do we go outside, following the pomp of the adulterer?
The ancient seducer deceives all through such things:
he sends in luxuries, through which he may destroy the sons of the Most High;
he sends in games, [to make them] go to bloody shows
or to very obscene ones, [so that] the chaste may know unchaste things.
If one had been chaste, he advances from there into unchastity,
and those things please and smile [on him] which then make trial with evil joys.
In these luxuries the firstborn people lived
and were always departing from God's law, monstrous.
To cleanse them God often sent his nurslings,
so that they might set them right again, depraved as they were, for the Highest.
They never wished to receive the divine words,
but in their own will they always raged, foolish.
They slaughtered unjustly the righteous who rebuked them,
since they would not accept the bridle of heavenly discipline.
They saw Isaiah in two, stone Jeremiah in their arrogance,
behead John, cut the throat of Zechariah at the altar.
And he himself came too, who had been foretold by them,
and suffers, in the way he willed, in our likeness.
In whose death all prophecy was fulfilled;
Daniel had said that he was the last for the prophets.
He was the one on whose account the prophets sang as with a trumpet
that he would come to his own, whom his own would deny.
Ever improvident and kicking back with stiff neck,
while they reject [his] form, they lose the sacraments of the law.
His righteousness, born in humble flesh, did not break them,
nor such great goodness, nor his healing of the sick by a word.
O holy religion, O majesty so worthy of reverence,
whose medicine has so advanced upon the earth!
He cut no one with iron, he cured no one with a plaster,
but without torment at once healed by his word.
Seeing such things the Jews were troubled in mind,
who rather were led by envy into the zeal of spite,
not regarding the sayings of the prophets, buried [as they were],
that such a man would come who would scatter them.
Until the Lord should come, the prophets sang:
from the time he came, prophecy fell silent for the Jews.
After him they went into exile with hardened heart,
nor even now do they discern why they have suffered such things.
It had been foretold to them by Isaiah the prophet
and likewise by Daniel that they would lose the land;
which, however, would not become deserted thereafter
until the leader of the city should hang on wood within it.
How suddenly glory shone forth upon a nation,
so that a people came to be, a people that was not before!
Was not Esau astonished, beloved by his father,
that that younger brother should take the birthright?
So neither could the synagogue recognise the time,
when and under what leader it would fall from its own possession;
as it was written, that the bird knows its seasons,
but this people has not understood that I am present.
It came to pass that the ruler of heaven himself should come:
according to the scriptures he was not reckoned [anything] by them.
The Lord had foreknown this, as one who knows all things;
therefore he foretold these things through the mouths of the prophets.
A race exceedingly stiff-necked and always rebelling,
while it claimed the primacy for itself, had its cause cut off.
In their course he set the gentiles to be;
he had said this before: 'The nations will hope in him.'
For he himself is the stone set in the foundations of Zion,
so that whoever believed in it should have eternal life.
Daniel signifies that this holy of holies is to be anointed
and that after him the royal chrism is to be destroyed.
David said that he would be fastened with nails, silent:
'They dug through', he says, 'my hands and feet.'
Solomon also prophesies so openly about him,
that the Jews would say: 'Let us kill the righteous one!'
Jeremiah likewise shows the cross figuratively,
[with them] saying: 'Come, let us put wood into his bread!'
And Moses, their leader, proclaims to them:
'Before your eyes your life will hang, slain.'
Here the Father came in the Son, one God everywhere:
nor was he called Father unless he had been made Son.
For he did not leave heaven in order to appear on earth,
but, as he arranged, his majesty was seen on earth;
by his own power he caused himself to be born in the flesh
* * may make one fringe.
Now the flesh was God, in which the power of God was acting.
What of the prophets' singing that the invisible would be seen,
so that such great splendour would also become man for us?
Nor would our people have sprung forth into a new law,
had the Almighty not ordained it beforehand concerning us.
This was the Almighty, in whose name the nations
would wholly believe, as the prophet Isaiah said:
'A man shall arise in Israel from the root of Jesse;
in him the nations will hope', by whose sign they are protected.
And another said that he would be a witness throughout the world,
that he himself would be revealed as prince to the nations.
In the psalms it is sung: 'The Lord has reigned from the wood;
let the earth exult, let the many islands rejoice.'
So too the true blessing of the patriarch Jacob
came forth upon the nations: 'He will be the hope of the nations', he says.
Under heaven there is no other name preferred except Christ's,
in whose name the nations everywhere have believed.
We are not persuaded to believe for the sake of a time that is closed,
but for the sake of the time to come, living in eternity.
This is the hope we must hope for, to enjoy the everlasting,
not these things, which, frail, quickly change our joys.
Though riches be before your eyes to be enjoyed lavishly,
you are shut out from them when perishable death takes their place;
or if you live on long, you yourself shudder at living,
or if your health is bad, what is life to you?
All that we live under this age is torment;
hence, then, our hope must be sought in the future:
to this God urges, to this the law, to this the passion of Christ,
that we should believe we will rise again in a new age.
So God's law cries out: when the Most High should become humble,
hell would give way, so that Adam might be raised from death.
The Lord, pitying his own creature, went down into the tomb,
and so by hidden means he emptied the strongholds of death.
The Lord crept up, hidden, on the ancient robber
and willed to suffer, so as to lay him low the more.
He indeed, bold and always savage as an enemy,
while he hopes to rage against a man, is conquered by the Highest.
By the very thing through which the malign one had first laid man low in death,
by that he was defeated; whence life comes to us.
Adam, having tasted the apple, was ordered to die and died;
through whose sin all of us likewise die in the same way.
But again the Lord said: 'If he takes from the tree of life,
let him live for ever in honour.'
Death was in a tree, and in a tree life lay hidden,
on which God the Lord hung, the finder of our life.
This the Lord had foretold to be the tree of life,
so that whoever believes in him is as if he took from it.
And he takes and sweetly tastes the precepts of the most high God
and departs from death, since he rises again the stronger.
Whoever believes in Christ tastes of the tree of life,
on which the Lord was hung, as foretold by Moses.
This same one Isaiah declares to be humble
and greatly cast down, as if he were in the form of a slave:
'And we saw him, and he was not of splendid appearance,
a man laid low in affliction, knowing how to bear all things.
He suffers for us and carries away our sins,
and for our crime God handed him over.
He, when he was tormented, was silent like a lamb at the altar.'
This was no longer [mere] man, but God was flesh for us;
by which it plainly appears that this name of God was to arise
which is now held a glorious name among the nations.
This the prophet Malachi sings, who is himself also an angel,
when he also rejects the sacrifices of the Jews, saying:
Your sacrifice will not be acceptable to me,
but in every place the nations offer to my name,
among whom my excellent name is magnified,
who offer to my name purely, without blood.
For he himself was lowly, hiding under a great name,
he who cries out concerning himself through the prophets' mouths:
"I am not stubborn," he says, "nor do I speak against the one who harms [me];
my back too I have set to the whips for beating,
and my cheeks to be struck by wicked palms
I offered, nor did I turn my face from their spittle."
It has struck many as folly that God suffered such things,
that the creator of the world should be proclaimed crucified.
So it pleased him, using no one's counsel —
nor could another [do it] — to come thus for us.
The enemy, being envious, devised death,
which the Lord drank down by suffering, rising again from the underworld.
For this reason he did not wish to reveal what he was,
but said that he was the Son sent by the Father.
So he himself had handed down to the prophets that he should be spoken of,
that God on earth should be the Son of the Most High.
This too he himself proclaims aloud, when he was lowly in the flesh,
and he bears witness to the Father, so as to confirm the prophets' mouths.
We read that such a man would rise from Israel:
"And he is a man," it says, "and who has known him among them?"
Jeremiah says: "This is our God; [none is] equal [to him];
after this he was also seen on earth, living among men."
And Isaiah: "You are God, and we did not know it;
and God is in you, and besides you no other is held [God]."
And who would come to the setting [of the sun], by the law of the prophets?
"Sing to the Lord; God is the name of him who comes!"
And the forty-fourth psalm says of him:
"I shall be exalted among the nations with a great name."
And elsewhere we read: "Today I have begotten you, son;
ask, and I will give you, and you shall have the nations as heirs."
Surely it is now plain who is God and who is in him,
and in whose name we nations everywhere should believe:
this was said to my Christ, whose right hand I hold:
"Let the nations hear, and let him rule the nations."
What need is there of more, when the matter is proved so openly,
when the people that is censured now rejoices in him?
But those wretches who embellish empty tales
and defame [him] as a magician, would have mocked the beaks of those who sing.
What shall I call them? Before they had been scattered,
neither exile nor slavery itself broke them.
If a magician had come, why then did the prophets sing
that he would come from heaven, to be himself the hope of the nations?
If they prophesy falsely of them that they would lose their land,
which has befallen them, so then would things about him also be false.
But because they have always been spurned, since they were bloody,
they rebel against their own Lord, calling [him] a magician.
Nor will they hear what the prophets said against them,
that they would not understand at all, even at the very end.
God himself described them: "With closed heart
let them neither see with their eyes nor understand with hardened heart;
for the heart of this wicked people has grown fat,
so that they recognise nothing, until they are healed by my word."
It was foretold that God would be born in the flesh for us,
so that their torment would deservedly be greater:
"Behold, God himself will give you a sign from on high:
a virgin will conceive, and the earth will bring forth the heavenly one;
and let him be called Emmanuel," he had commanded them;
which in the Latin tongue unfolds as 'God with us'.
Hear that he would be nourished on honey and butter,
and would take Samaria before he spoke a word.
But this is a hidden story, which the learned unroll:
that a little suckling child would seize spoils without battle.
His passion was foretold beforehand in such a way
that God would become capable of suffering, with his blood poured out.
Isaiah says: "Like a sheep led to the altar,
he did not cry out with his voice; he bore all things patiently."
He is fastened with nails, as David had foretold long ago;
and they gave him vinegar to drink, according to the scriptures.
"And over my garments," he said, "they cast lots";
which was done, and we read that all things were accomplished in him.
And there was darkness too, for three hours from the sixth,
and the day hastened, bringing on the stars of night.
This had been foretold to happen through the prophet Amos:
that it would suddenly hide itself during the holy feast.
O wicked offspring, * * with deceitful face!
"I have begotten children," God said, "who would deny me."
And he said: "Hear the voice of the trumpet." — "We will not," they say.
This Ezekiel says: "So the nations will hear from afar."
With one heading I want to touch on the book of Deuteronomy:
"You nations shall be at the head; for the unbelieving [shall be] behind."
If the rebels indeed reject all the things said above,
do you know what they set against [them], when the matter is stated so openly?
See now, then, you who until now have floated in doubt,
that the nations were first in the scripture of the Lord.
Now, then, it is right to believe in him whom the books point out,
not in empty idols, which are worshipped in vain for life,
nor to join those who are given to pleasure and without restraint,
who love luxuries more than the commands of the Highest.
One fault is not enough for those who will not believe,
but they defame [him] further: "We cast him into a pit."
Wherefore the Lord too, angered, pours on them [this rebuke]:
"Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations," he says.
If he was cast into a pit, why then is it proclaimed that he rose again?
"From the underworld, Lord, you have restored my soul";
"I slept," he says, "and took my sleep secure;
by the help of the Lord I arose, having suffered no harm."
And again he says: "You will not leave [me] in the underworld,
nor will you let your holy one see destruction."
Here he says resoundingly: "Son of the prophet, I ascend,
so that I may tell of the Lord most high, who suffered through misery."
And in the book of Psalms the Lord's death is proclaimed,
not, as they think, David speaking of himself.
Or if they think that, does everything he said fit?
David was not scourged, nor raised on a cross.
What? Do the Jews prophesy in the manner of Saturn?
Do they gather into fables, when [the prophecy] now turns against them?
Did they not slap him like a criminal, raised on the cross?
To the unknowing, the unlearned, the ignorant they invent such things.
"Who is that God, whom we fastened to a cross?" they say,
unwilling to look at the scriptures, blinded in heart.
Behold, another prophet sings, repeating it again,
by whose voice nonetheless such a decree is proclaimed:
"Now I will arise," says the Lord, "now I will be glorified,
now I will be exalted, whom before you saw lowly;
now you understand, now will be your confusion:
you think vain things, therefore fire will hold you."
This Isaiah says. Then so the majesty itself too,
when it was in the flesh, declares itself who it was:
"No one, though he tries, will be able to take away my soul,
but I lay it down of myself, freely, by my own decree.
I myself have the power of laying it down,
and of taking it up again I have power over it."
Yet more openly is the death of the just one proclaimed,
so that it may be more evident that the Jews are hardened:
"Behold, the just one perishes, and no one at all understands;
but the burial of this beloved one will be in peace."
Why do they defame [him] as let down into a pit,
when we read that he was given over to burial?
Shameful, cruel, blind, proud,
they who ought rather to mourn over the deed applaud!
For Solomon, inspired, prophesies of him,
and goes on further to show the just one more fully:
"Let us beset the just one, if he seems burdensome [to us],
who strongly resists, opposed to our works;
he reproaches [us] that nothing at all is kept by our law,
and further he affirms that he is the Son of the Most High.
In every way he rejects [us] and judges [us] to be triflers;
he keeps himself apart from us and goes other ways;
he calls us unclean and introduces other rules of right,
and rejoices that the Lord is his father in heaven.
So, if his words are true, let us test [them];
let us try this God, seeing what happens to him;
let us question him, quiet as he is, with every torment;
let us condemn him to a most shameful death," saying.
When they had done these things, wagging their heads they urged:
"Let the Father save him, or let him come down from there!"
To show openly that they were blind, Solomon,
as if he were telling it now, censures them for having done such things:
"While they think these things, they were led into abominable error;
their malice blinded them to rage."
See, because they are themselves blind and call others so,
Solomon said of them: "They did not know the secrets of God."
Whatever all the former witnesses said
was done in Christ. Or would they say [it was done] in another?
If they wish to do that, deceiving with their mouths,
let them mock themselves; let them see it fulfilled in him.
Who was that just one of whom the prophets sang,
since no one is just on earth, unless he had come from heaven?
For David, the prince, sinned by loving a girl;
Solomon also sinned; and yet they repented.
Since these so famous and distinguished kings of theirs
were not just, but themselves sang of the just one,
nor did the prophet Isaiah say such things of himself,
who was cut with a saw by King Manasseh.
One was stoned, another slaughtered at the altar,
another Herod ordered beheaded in prison.
All these prophets were destroyed by a different death,
whereas the Lord hung on wood, by the voice of Moses:
'God is not hung up as a man,' he declares beforehand;
'Nor does he suffer threats as a son of man,' he says.
So when the Lord himself had come, following these things,
'I must,' he said, 'be rejected,' by the voice of Moses.
But I do not pluck the whole, only the highest peaks,
so that the ignorant may more easily learn the truth.
But these wicked ones, who seek to live by deceit,
bloodstained once and for all, persist in inventing empty things.
They befool the foolish into fading away further by their words,
that he was crucified, when this was how it had to be for him.
For he arranged it so because of the ruin of the first-made [man];
not only for him, but for us too he came from heaven.
He established a new people, firm in his name;
Christ fulfilled all things according to the prophecies.
'Behold, I make new things,' Isaiah cries concerning him,
'and let no one think on former things or follow the ancient ones.'
These new things have come forth today under our law:
that we Gentiles have believed in Christ, by the word of Moses.
He had foretold that there would be two peoples,
and indeed he said that the lesser people would excel.
But these, full of wickedness, now in desperate fury:
'The law was given to us,' they say; 'where have you come from?'
If they oppose us, they think they are also resisting the Highest,
who willed to be good to us * * ?
Nor do these stiff-necked ones, with bristles raised, consider
that they always tortured the innocent, shunning the law.
So they did to God what they were used to doing, cruel as they were,
and they still dare to call themselves sons of the Highest.
How he rose again I have noted above;
I spoke not with my own voice, but prophetic words.
He had foretold everything about himself to the disciples:
how he would suffer at the hands of the people, with Peter denying [him];
and that he would rise from the tomb on the third day,
he had said this too, and he fulfilled all that he said.
But when he had risen, he came himself to the apostles
and stood in their midst: 'Peace to you,' he said.
Among those disciples at prayer one was not present;
when they told him, he began to disbelieve, and added:
'Unless I first put my finger where the nails were,
or where he was struck by the lance, I do not believe.'
Then on the Lord's day he came back to them again
and stood in their midst: 'Peace to you,' he said.
And at once he approaches Thomas, that unbeliever:
'Come closer and touch my body as before.
I am not a shade, such as the dead are held to be:
a shade leaves no footprint; look at the wound.'
He stretched out his palms; and the other began to touch [them],
and his hand into the side, where the lance had been fixed,
he put, and then threw himself down, praying:
'You are truly my God and Lord!' To which he [replied]:
'Because you have seen these things, you have believed; but happy are those
who come after, who believe having only heard the name.'
Forty days in succession he spent with them;
he taught them many things that would come upon the world.
After his ascension they worked many miracles;
with a word they healed the sick in the name of Christ.
If he had been such as these faithless ones say,
mighty works would not have been done through him at the word of witnesses.
He ascended into the heavens, as scripture too had sung:
'Receive the king, you princes, in the heights of heaven!'
What more need is there to recite everything from the law?
These things are enough for the untaught, to be regarded with a good heart.
But if they will not come to know God by reading these things,
let them blame themselves for where they have come, to where they do not wish.
Virgil is read, or Cicero, or Terence likewise;
they do nothing but [train] the mind; of life, besides, there is silence.
What good is it to pursue worldly things in vain on earth,
and to know of the vices of kings and of their wars?
Or to come to know the mad forum, skilled in law,
since justice totters unless perhaps it is steered by a bribe?
Though he be an advocate, though a divine orator,
he will gain nothing at death if, while living, he denied Christ.
Rather let him first ask where his life is being brought!
So he would be wise, even if otherwise he is reproached.
They read the laws and learn wonderful pleadings,
but in pleading they overreach the wretches for whom they speak.
Unhappy is he who has fallen into their mouths:
they carry off the praise, and he a victory with losses.
The wretch stands mute in the middle, aching more within;
they thunder with their mouths, and he in silence with his coins.
Meanwhile the polished voice roars day after day,
and often a case is made better by giving a little more.
Hence the wise man seeks his fee, hence he rejoices to win;
even if he acts wrongly, so long as he is the victor, he is sick.
He does nothing about his own case while he strives for gain;
he takes on another's hope and puts his own behind him.
Many are carried off by success in the forest of the world;
while they rejoice in brief things, they stay far from the grace of Christ;
while they covet much with the eye, while they seek to increase,
God is nothing to them, only the life of the world.
Toil is spent for the belly, a daily contest for it,
and they scorn the true contest for eternal salvation.
Whoever keeps watch, as it were, over his money-bag is praised as sharp;
but he who follows God is judged dung by them.
O happy beyond measure, if anyone shuns worldly things!
Let him be a fool to others, so long as he is wise to God most high.
This is the whole hope: to believe in God, who hung on wood;
a shameful thing though it is, yet useful for the life to come.
For that first people was deceived by this:
that he spoke of a son, though he himself is the God of old.
He went before them in the pillar of cloud and fire,
when he freed them from Egypt to the last man.
He commands a cruel crime concerning the only son,
to test Abraham, to whom 'Spare [him]!' was said from heaven
by an angel. And he is God, and made himself man as well,
and whatever he wills, he will do, so that dumb things speak.
He made his she-ass speak to Balaam as he sat [on her],
and a dog, so that it said to Simon: 'You are called by Peter!'
So that many might speak of him as Paul preached,
he made a lion speak to the people with a divine voice.
Then, what our nature itself does not allow,
he made an infant in its fifth month speak out before the crowd.
He was to come mingled with our blood,
so as to seem a man, but God lay hidden in the flesh.
'No elder will come, nor an angel,' said Isaiah,
'but the Lord himself will come to show himself to us.'
Him the sea feared, him the winds, him Tartarus itself;
every creature recognised the hidden Lord.
Only the wicked people raised its neck against him:
'God forbid that the Lord should have come thus, in such a form!'
He walked on the waves of the sea as on land,
and commands the winds, to make the sea calm.
He broke the law of Tartarus with a word, there in person,
and raises from the tomb Lazarus, stinking on the fourth day.
For to one who was being carried out, when he met him:
'Arise, young man,' he said; and he rose up from the bier.
The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, entreated by her father,
already lifeless, he raises up while they mourned.
He made the mute speak and, above all, the deaf hear,
and the man blind from the womb see the light of day.
After thirty-eight years he ordered the paralytic to rise,
whom they marvelled at, carrying his pallet on his neck.
By touching his garment, [a woman] with a flow [of blood] was healed.
He broke five loaves for five thousand men,
and again fed four thousand from seven.
That the Lord might show more fully that he was present,
he changed water, so that it became the best wine.
He had been invited to a wedding together with his mother;
since he was asked to help when the wine ran out,
he then ordered the jars to be filled quickly with water,
which he first tasted, and so ordered it served.
Not even so could they recognise the Lord by his deeds,
but they raged to destroy him by death as a criminal.
This he allows, since he had resolved to suffer so;
yet if they believe, then at last they will have pardon.
This is the firstborn, foretold long before by the prophets,
to be called on earth the offspring of the Most High.
Happy those among men who place their hope in him,
for the foolish shun him as a curse.
Eternity is prepared for him who believes in Christ,
so that man may be God's companion, living after death.
The law and the prophets teach who are worthy of God's heavens,
and to whom the hidden golden ages are revealed.
Through so many prophets the cry is raised about the Son of God,
and the sons of God first called have closed their eyes;
who, when the crime was done, did not remember it in their reading,
but went on persistently saying: 'We are the chosen!'
They still befool the profane into going to baths,
whom they themselves make clean, [they say], to please God most high.
Water washes off dirt, not the inner wickedness of the heart,
nor could rites, however performed, wash the sacrilegious clean.
The Lord did not command this, to offer holy things to the wicked;
and he spoke again, that they be kept clean from idols:
'Let no one make himself an image of a demon,' he says;
for he also told them: 'Do not serve idols.'
If God commanded that idols be strictly avoided,
why do they deceive the Gentiles that they are pure by washings?
Rather, when they receive such people, they ought to teach them
to serve no others, but only to please the Highest.
While they seek to cast a shadow over the crime of Christ's death,
they open the doors everywhere, so that people come in to them.
Hence, then, they perish who think that by water they can be pure
and become God's, though they were before accomplices of a robber.
Now he worships any empty thing, now he seeks holy things;
that ignorant man does not know where to run first,
and he serves idols, then seeks the thirtieth-day rites;
now he follows unleavened bread, he who before had sat chaste.
It did not please God that [men] be partakers with demons,
He who instituted the law, so that from there a passage might be made.
Two ways are set before you: choose which you wish,
for you will not split yourself so as to go by both;
but still you must seek out the right one of them;
be more careful, so that you do not fall into the jaws of robbers.
Seek the one God, who seeks no sacrifices,
so that, though destroyed, you may rise again when the age is renewed.
Why do you heed the wicked and judge the holy to be unjust,
[the wicked] who show you not one word from the law?
They recount the mighty work of God, which He did among them;
for of their own wicked deeds they refuse to speak,
always murderers, and always with bloody hands,
whom the Lord could never tame by warning.
It had been enough for them, through sloth, to have done so much,
and to say: 'So it was written; now it is right to believe.'
But the Lord Himself darkened their understanding,
He hardened them as [He hardened] Pharaoh among them;
and He said that He would not hear their prayers,
and in anger He cast them out of their land.
Though He had indeed called them sons before,
He had required that [His] children live with a good heart;
for a father rejoices when his son is good to him;
but if he turns out wicked, he curses his child with hatred.
No one tolerates a son who is hostile to himself;
all love is shut out from a cruel child,
nor does [the father] make him sole heir of his goods,
and if he can use them up first, he rejoices at his expense.
An impious and savage offspring, a tyrant over his property,
the father, provoked by him, cannot bear even to meet.
What do these presume, though they are [only] adopted, saying:
'Out of every people we are dearest to the Highest'?
One who is ever a parricide of his father and proud against him,
can he be dear, or be called heir by right?
If fathers in the flesh detest such children,
how much more the Lord, who has sons in abundance to choose from!
To gentle, humble children, full of obedience,
are the goods divided, not to the impious or to tyrants.
The Jews had plainly been adopted as sons,
but in the testament they obtained the name of impious.
Let them reckon for themselves: bloodstained by the crime they committed,
how could they possibly share in the goods?
Why do they gnash their teeth at us, why do they envy us as heirs?
Had they done good, they too would have had a share in the legacy.
Even today they are not silent and refuse to believe in Christ,
who had been foretold to them in the law as the bringer of salvation;
of whom you have already heard how the prophets sang:
that the Lord would come to earth, whom the nations will worship.
Surely they urge us to recognise this very one as the Highest,
who renews man and forgives former sins.
For He Himself also threatens the worshippers of gods:
'He who sacrifices to idols will perish in the second death.'
Whoever, then, follows gods fashioned in gold,
silver or stone, wood, or cast in bronze,
will be thrown, wretched, with them into the fire, restored [in body],
and does not die off there, but the wicked one pays in torments.
There are men like cattle in this life,
who refuse to take the bridle of the highest God, and wander;
though they themselves cannot bear such things from their slaves,
into whose blood they often go down, cruel as they are.
Speaking, they add: 'There is nothing after our death;
while we live, this is it,' and they bend down like swine;
'Let no luxury pass us by in our lifetime;
while there is time of life, let us enjoy all the things of the world.'
Undisciplined, they reject the mercy of God,
pursuing revelry, as if this life were the only one.
So they turn back from God, who promises that [we] live forever:
they fight against the good, when one ought to fight the wicked.
We all plainly went astray, persuaded by the world,
but by the grace of the Lord we are called to believe the law.
For this reason He came and won trophies in secret,
and God was man, so as to have us in the future.
But very many perish who think they can please both,
idols and God, though no one can please two.
There is one God in heaven, of heaven, earth and sea,
whom Moses taught had hung on the wood for us.
Hence some, slothful, go astray [about Him] who suffered such things,
not attentive enough to the secret mystery of God.
Through the envy of the devil death entered the world,
which God destroyed in secret, born of a virgin.
At this birth the blind Jews lose their wits;
they make fools of the foolish, bloodstained by the crime they committed.
No one can offer any excuse afterwards,
since now the opportunity to believe is given us.
The Lord did not come from heaven to earth in vain,
but came to make a people called by His name.
If anyone has not confessed Him in this life,
he loses even what he has lived, and in punishment cries out too late;
or surely, while he hopes, waiting to believe when grey-haired,
he dies and is shut out the longer from eternal life.
So we ought to turn our minds to Him quickly,
who promises to give us back life after death.
Besides, He adds this: that we shall be immortal,
and enjoy, by seeing, what the eye had not seen before.
These things will come when six thousand years are complete,
at which time I hope that we ourselves will be on the shore of the harbour.
Then man will rise, brought back in the course of the sun,
and rejoices in God, remembering what he was before;
he who, as he heard while frail in his former flesh,
being incorruptible, recognises what was promised before.
Marvelling that such glory has come to man, he says:
'As I heard before, so I see each thing.'
All cry this together, raised up from the underworld:
'Just as we heard before, look, we see!'
All pain will leave the body, and the sore will leave it too,
nor will there be any anxiety, but always joys.
Whoever believes in the three and perceives that one is present,
he will be everlasting, reborn into the eternal ages.
But some say this: 'When do we suppose these things will come?'
Hear in brief after what events they will follow.
Many signs indeed will mark the end of so great a plague,
but the beginning will be our seventh persecution.
Look, he already knocks at the door and girds himself with a sword,
he who will soon cross the river with the Goths bursting in.
King Apollyon will be with them, dreadful by name,
who is to break up the persecution of the saints by arms.
He goes to Rome with many thousands of his people,
and by God's decree takes captive those subdued in part.
For then many of the senators will weep as captives
and blaspheme the God of heaven, conquered by a barbarian.
Yet these gentiles feed the Christians everywhere,
seeking them out rather as brothers, full of joy.
For the luxurious and those who worship empty idols
they persecute indeed, and put the senate under the yoke.
These evils befall those who persecuted the beloved:
for five months they are slaughtered under this enemy.
Meanwhile, at that very time, Cyrus arises,
to terrify the enemy and free the senate from there.
He returns from the underworld, who had been snatched from his reign
and long kept, known by his former body.
We say that this is the Nero of old,
who once punished Peter and Paul in the city.
He himself returns again at the very end of the age
from hidden places, he who was reserved for this.
The senate itself marvels at him who was unseen;
when he appears, they will think him a god, as it were.
But before he comes, Elijah will prophesy
at the divided time, at the midpoint of the week.
When the period is complete, that abominable one follows,
whom the Jews too will then worship together with the Romans.
Although there will be another, whom they await from the east,
yet in our slaughter they will rage with King Nero.
So when Elijah prophesies in the land of Judaea,
and marks the people with a sign in the name of Christ;
since so many of them refuse to believe him,
in anger he prays the Most High that it should not rain from then on:
the sky will be shut from then and will not be wet with dew,
and in anger he also turns the rivers into blood.
The earth becomes barren and does not sweat water from its springs,
so that famine invades; there will then be plague in the world too.
Because he does these things, the Jews, tormented,
forge many false charges against him,
and first inflame the senate to rise up in wrath,
and say that Elijah acts as an enemy to the Romans.
Then at once the senate, stirred up by them,
entreat Nero with prayers and wicked gifts:
'Remove the enemies of the people from human affairs,
through whom our gods are trampled and not worshipped.'
And he, filled with fury and by the senate's prayers,
seizes the prophets from the east by the public post.
To satisfy them, or rather the Jews,
he sacrifices these first and so goes out against the churches.
At their martyrdom a tenth part of the city collapses,
and fully seven thousand men perish there.
But the Lord on the fourth day lifts them into the air,
whom those had forbidden to be buried as they lay;
and they are raised from the ground, made immortal out of death,
and their enemies look up at them going through the air.
Not even so are they terrified, but they grow more savage within
towards the people of Christ, cursing them with all hatred.
For the Most High hardened their abominable hearts,
as He had once hardened Pharaoh's ears.
So then this harsh and wicked king, Nero, [once] put to flight,
orders the Christian people to be driven from the city itself,
and he adds to himself two Caesars as partners,
with whom to persecute this people with dreadful fury.
They also send edicts through all the judges everywhere,
that they should make this race of men be without the name of Christ.
They command too that incense be set before the images,
and that, so that no one may hide, all should come forward wearing garlands.
If in this story a believer refused to go,
it will be a blessed thing; but if not, he becomes one of the crowd.
There will then be no day of peace, nor offering to Christ,
but blood flows everywhere, which I am unable to describe;
for tears overcome me, my hand fails, my heart trembles,
although it is fitting for martyrs to bear so many deaths;
over sea, over lands, over islands and hiding places
they search for a long time, and lead the accursed off as victims.
These things Nero will then do, and for the whole space of three years
and half a year he completes the appointed times;
for whose crime a deadly vengeance will come,
so that the city and that people will be handed over together with him,
and the empire taken away, which was filled with wickedness,
which for a long time wore everyone down with cruel taxes.
There will rise up again, at the downfall of this Nero,
a king from the east, with four nations from there,
and he invites to himself very many nations against the city,
to bring him help, though he himself is very strong,
and he will fill the sea with ships with many thousands,
and if anyone meets him, he will be slaughtered with the sword;
and first he takes captive Tyre and Sidon, subdued,
for from that the neighbouring nations grow faint with terror.
Here plague, here wars, here famine, here harsh tidings
are mingled together, so that there is confusion of mind.
Meanwhile a trumpet suddenly sounds a roar from heaven,
whose sound in every place troubles the heart.
And then a fiery four-horse chariot will be seen among the stars,
and a running torch, to announce fire to the nations.
Then the river Euphrates is dried up entirely,
so that a way may be prepared for the king with those nations.
Persians, Medes, Chaldaeans too, Babylonians will come,
pitiless and swift, who do not know how to feel pity for anyone.
So when this one, rising, has begun to come from there,
Nero and the senate are thrown into confusion at the sight close by.
And those three Caesars will go to resist [him]:
these he slaughters and gives to the birds for food.
Their armies must needs worship the victor,
with whom, returning to the city with changed minds,
they plunder the temples and whatever is within the city;
they sack [it] and slaughter men with vast bloodshed;
at last they bring it down bare, setting it on fire,
so that not even a trace of it appears any more.
At its ruin the hearts of the powerful waste away,
and, stupefied, they cannot find out in what time they are.
She used to rejoice, but the whole earth groaned;
yet scarcely does a worthy requital come to her.
She mourns for ever, who boasted herself eternal,
and her tyrants too are already then judged by the Highest.
The time stands ripe for the end, with Rome smoking,
and the reward will come, apportioned to the merits of places.
From there, however, the victor proceeds into the land of Judaea,
whom the Jews themselves had watched conquer Rome.
He performs many signs, so that they may believe,
since the wicked one has been sent to lead them astray;
yet a voice of the Highest, sounding from heaven, rebukes him.
A man from Persia, he says that he is immortal.
For us Nero has become Antichrist, that one for the Jews;
these two are always prophets at the very end.
Nero is the ruin of the city, this one of the whole earth;
about whom, however, I put forward a few things which I have read in secret writings.
Meanwhile, too late, the Jews too become displeased with him,
and they murmur together that they have been deceived by fraud.
Together they cry out to heaven, weeping aloud,
that the true God may help them from on high.
Then God almighty, to complete all that I have said,
will bring forth a people hidden for a long time.
They are Jews, shut in by a river beyond Persia,
whom God willed to stay there until the end.
Captivity brought them to be there;
of the twelve tribes, nine and a half dwell there.
There is no lying there, nor any hatred;
therefore no son dies before his parents;
nor do they lament or mourn the dead after our fashion,
since they await the resurrection to come.
They do not eat any living thing with added foods,
but only vegetables, which is without blood being shed.
Full of justice, they live with undefiled body,
and among them the impious horoscope does not exert its powers.
Fevers do not come upon them, nor cruel chills,
since they obey all things of the pure law;
which we ourselves too shall follow, living purely;
only death and toil were present, for the rest were deaf.
So this people, which is now stored away outside,
when the river is dried up, will return to the land of Judaea;
and with them God will come to fulfil the promises,
and they exult along the whole journey with God present.
All things grow green before them, all things rejoice,
creation itself is glad to receive the saints:
in every place springs rise up to be ready [for them],
wherever the people of the Highest walks with heavenly terror.
The clouds make a shade [for them], so that they are not troubled by the sun,
and so that they do not grow weary, the mountains themselves lie flat beneath them;
for an angel of the Most High will be sent ahead before them,
to give them peaceful leadership as they go.
These walk lightly without toil as they go,
and like lions, wherever they pass, they lay everything waste.
Nor indeed will any nation be able to resist them,
if it makes war, since God himself is with them.
They conquer nations, they also bring down cities,
by God's permission they empty all the settlements,
and they enrich themselves with gold or silver by plunder,
and so, honoured, they sing hymns together.
Soon, however, they hasten to the holy city of their fathers,
for that terrible tyrant will take fright,
and he flees to the kings of the North with a great commotion,
from where he seizes a people, so as to stand as if fighting back.
But when the rebels hasten against the army of God,
they are laid on the ground by the angels when battle is joined
(and the adulterer is seized, and his false prophet
are sent alive into the lake under fiery punishment).
Of these, those who are leaders, governors or envoys,
the wicked are reduced to the place of servants of the saints.
Meanwhile the saints enter the holy settlement,
to receive the promises of God, rejoicing without end.
They entreat God for the dead, that they may rise again,
as he himself promised long ago concerning the first resurrection.
God will then begin to be angry with his enemies,
since the appointed day has come for the wicked.
But when he begins to judge the world by fire,
the fire both avoids the godly and will fall upon the ungodly.
Scarcely a few remain to tell of such deeds,
and those who are kept back to serve the just escape.
After the persecution of the saints and so many deaths
the hateful, burning day is at hand to come.
Behold, [a trumpet] sounds in heaven, hoarse but echoing everywhere,
which terrifies the whole world falling into ruin.
The sun flees unawares, suddenly there is the likeness of night,
and God cries out: 'How long did you think I would bear [it]?'
At his given signal destruction will rush through the whole sky,
with the crash of thunder the onset of fire comes down.
Then thunderbolt after thunderbolt is hurled from the stars,
the fiery storm rages, kept back for so many years.
The deadly disaster roars, the earth trembles, roused,
and the whole human race cannot see where to turn.
The stars of heaven fall, the stars are judged with us:
the heavenly beings are troubled while the world's ruin is carried out.
There will then be no help, and crying out is vain;
no ship will take a person in, nor any hiding place;
nor do those help them whom before they worshipped as great:
each one busies himself for himself, but it will profit him nothing;
it will profit only those who have been marked by Christ;
there will be dew for them, but for the rest deadly punishment.
A part of the unbelievers is kept, gently burned,
so that their race may lament itself again at the last.
Wherever people turn, the fiery force seethes;
the very air of the world, which was pleasant before, is burned.
How many crashes of the sky assailing with thunderbolts shall I tell of,
when the wrath gathered over so many years is all poured out?
Here fire, here thunder, here whirlwinds, so many evils, rage,
and the sky is snatched by the sudden force of death into shadow.
In part the trembling earth loosens all its foundations,
in part thunderclaps burst apart strong ramparts;
and walls are scattered like dust into the air;
rocks fly, the roofs of houses are stripped by the winds.
Homelands are laid waste, every city is laid low
[...] give a kiss to the footprint.
So many crashes, such roarings and such ruins
who will be able to bear, or escape such great shipwrecks?
What will the wretched mother then do for her sweet little one?
Or if a father shows devotion to his son, what will it profit him?
Woe to those who flee from the Lord, woe too to the wicked without Christ,
of whom both those rejoicing and those weeping in piety are judged!
Moreover, all nature will lament with bellowings,
until the heavenly fury ceases, at last fulfilled.
Then for seven months the earth will be cleansed by fire,
and he who was lowly is seen coming from heaven.
With him will descend the angels of eternal brightness;
the tombs too will be burst open, the bodies of the just will rise up,
which the clouds snatch up and carry to meet Christ
in the air; the saints who are living receive the Lord.
He raises those too, so that they may see his glory,
whom they fixed to the cross; but he will give them back again to the depths.
Woe to those wretched ones! He who was killed by them is the witness.
That for their punishments, foreseeing, by deceit [...]
We do not sing these things out of envy, but we see them fixed.
While the just rejoice, [those others] are burned in hell;
David said of them: Lord, repay them [their] iniquities!
And if they do not believe, they will go away into the shadow of death. —
He could surely have prayed for joyful things for his people;
why did he rather wish: Let them go down alive below?
